title: Dark reactions that need light
question: Why does the Calvin cycle, nicknamed the dark reaction, depend on light?
hook: A reaction nicknamed dark still waits on products made in the light.
idea: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent reactions to turn carbon dioxide into sugars, so it runs when light is available.

beats.prompt: Three carbon dioxide molecules go through the cycle and make six G3P molecules. How much does the cell keep as a net gain?

choices.label: All six G3P
choices.feedback: Most of the six are needed to rebuild the starting compound.

choices.label: Three G3P, one for each carbon dioxide
choices.feedback: Each carbon dioxide yields two G3P, and most are recycled.

beats.explain: Five of the six G3P regenerate RuBP, leaving a net gain of one G3P per three CO₂.

beats.prompt: Put these steps of RuBP regeneration in order.
items: Triose phosphate isomerase turns one G3P into DHAP
Aldolase and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase join G3P and DHAP into fructose 6-phosphate
Transketolase removes two carbons from F6P, giving E4P
Phosphoribulokinase turns RuP into RuBP, completing the cycle
beats.explain: Regeneration starts with G3P becoming DHAP, then F6P forms and loses two carbons as E4P, and finally RuP is phosphorylated into RuBP.

beats.prompt: Which stage does each description belong to?
items: Converts carbon dioxide into organic compounds
beats.explain: The first stage captures light to make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle uses those compounds to convert carbon dioxide into organic compounds.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: In the first stage, light-dependent reactions make ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle uses those compounds to turn carbon dioxide into sugars.
Because of the name dark reaction, the cycle can run all night on leftover NADPH.
In the dark, plants instead release sucrose into the phloem from starch reserves.
beats.explain: NADPH is short-lived and comes from the light-dependent reactions, so the cycle does not occur in the dark.
